body:
ehaugsja@cs.umass.edu wrote:
> 
> Ross writes:
> > It is a matter of common sense
> > that if all the factories were destroyed
> > and books burned as he insists must
> > be done,  that there would be no
> > way to suppress the emergence
> > of technology anew absent such
> > social controls.
> 
> But isn't it the point of ISAIF that all the social controls, marketing,
> etc, etc. that they hate can only be justified if they are in pursuit of
> the goal to end all goals -- destruction of modern technology and the
> return of wild nature?
> 
>   "202. It would be hopeless for revolutionaries to try to attack the system
>   without using SOME modern technology. If nothing else they must use the
>   communications media to spread their message. But they should use modern
>   technology for only ONE purpose: to attack the technological system."
> 
> So, once the revolution is underway, the control would hopefully not be
> needed, and because the people in charge would not be power-hungry leftists
> (like himself) they would then step down and let wild nature (Mitch) take
> over.

	I think Ross is making another point, about the stability of the
post-revolutionary period.  Would the technological system simply emerge
again?  That possibility is conceded in ISAIF paragraphs 165 and 212:

"165."  "...It is impossible to predict what would emerge from such a
time of troubles, but at any rate the human race would be given a new
chance.  The greatest danger is that industrial society would begin to
reconstitute itself within the first few years after the breakdown..."

"212.  Would society EVENTUALLY evelope again toward an
industrial-technological form?  Maybe, but there is no use in worrying
about it, since we can't predict or control events 500 or 1,000 years in
the future.  Those problems must be dealt with by the people who will
live at that time."

Scott
